chapter: Washington clubs, Louis Jordan and Sarah Vaughan, 1949-54
title: London welcome and a BBC broadcast that starts when the BBC wants
summary: Greeted like royalty, they arrive early for the 8 o'clock broadcast and learn British radio starts when it pleases.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Anyway, we arrived at London and we were greeted just like what we felt like was royalty, because there were people waiting at the train station, and we were treated very well, taken to the hotels and given every courtesy. The London media and the agents and everything... Everything was just beautiful.

We stayed there for a couple of days before we actually went into rehearsal. One of the things first that sort of amazed Sarah and I was that before we actually went on this trip.... Well, while the tour was being set up... I would say we were actually there about three or four days before we went on the tour.. We were called to do a show on the BBC, the British Broadcasting Company. So they said that the broadcast would be at 8 o'clock. So, knowing this, Sarah and I, knowing how things are in the States here, we elected to get there a little before 7:30, just in case we had to time some numbers

So we got there. Everyone greeted us and they were standing around and drinking tea or coffee, and talking about our trip and whatever. So I'm watching the clock. Every now and then, Sarah would glance at me. And I just shrugged my shoulders. They knew what they were doing, I guess. So it comes on, it's 20 minutes of, a quarter of eight, and these British people were taking. Every now and then, something would come up, a funny story or something. Nobody's making a move!

Finally, it's 5 minutes to 8, nobody's still made a move, and then finally it's 8 o'clock and then 5 after 8. So by this time, I've got to say something. "Look, the show was supposed to be at 8 o'clock. What's going on?" He says, "Oh, don't worry about that. We're not like you people over there. The show goes on over here when we want to put it on."

Anyway, I think the show went on around 20 or 25 minutes after 8. Of course, after we found this out, we just relaxed, and when we went on, it wasn't a matter of timing what we did. They said, "Go on and do what you do." I think we had to do two or three tunes -- "the length of them doesn't matter." It was a very different kind of experience. Over here, where everything is timed, the place where you're going to stand sit, or everything is right down to the minute.
